  ↳ Cleaned up 4 duplicate keys in the glossary tooltip layer, and closed the hole in the checker that let them slip past a green board. The other three (meq/l, Supralife, glacial milk) were aliases that just re-spelled their own term in lowercase — dead weight, since the matcher already lowercases everything. I fixed the data and taught the gate to catch this whole class so it can never come back quietly. DATA — dashboard/assets/data/glossary.json (hand-authored, not sealed): - myelofibrosis: removed the mis-attributed "myelosclerosis" alias. The dedicated myelosclerosis entry stays canonical, so the hover now correctly reads "hardening and scarring of the bone marrow" (previously it resolved to myelofibrosis's wording). - mEq/L: removed the redundant self-alias "meq/l"; kept the distinct "meq". - SupraLife: removed the redundant self-alias "Supralife"; kept "SupraLife International". - Glacial Milk: removed the redundant self-alias "glacial milk" (aliases now []). git diff = 4 hunks, +2/-8, no CRLF churn. Re-scan = 0 colliding keys. Matcher-simulation confirms every lowercase form (glacial milk / meq/l / supralife) still resolves via the term's own lowercasing. GATE (R9 — fix the misfire WITH proof) — tools/invariants.py: - Added module-level _glossary_key_collisions(terms): every normalized (lowercased) key across term + aliases must be globally unique, because the runtime folds them into one Map where a repeat is a silent override. - Wired it into check_glossary_wellformed, REPLACING the old term-only "seen" check (which only compared term-vs-term and never looked at aliases — that is exactly why all four collisions passed). The new check subsumes the old one. Docstring corrected: "terms are unique" was untrue of the alias space. TEST — tools/test_glossary_wellformed.py: +6 key-space cases (alias==another-entry-term trips; self-alias-lowercase trips; shared-alias trips; duplicate-term still trips; case-insensitive collision trips; distinct-and-clean passes). 28/28 cases pass. VERIFICATIONS: node tools/build.mjs (main.js 6.1mb, glossary re-inlined) · invariants.py 77/77 (glossary_wellformed green: 219 defs, 2 anchored number-exempt) · render_probe_knowledge PASS (0 page errors, 82 glosses resolve) · Python matcher-simulation proof. (SELENIUM/SULPHUR/TIN/VANADIUM) -- so positional indexing cannot be right there; (b) its range REPEATS the unit ("20,000 IU - 300,000 IU"), so the group parser split ONE column into TWO, making the under-filled row LOOK full and hiding fault (a). ## 2026-07-17 08:58 UTC-05:00 · session-end · corpus
Session closed for a fresh one on 'the others'. Audit + purge + source-fix landed: 1336 claims at kv=345, board 76/76. The number was 29, not 300+ — and the biggest error found was the audit's own scoping, which cost 43.5% of its flags
  ↳ Session closed at Luneth's instruction, to open a fresh one for "the others." Everything is committed and pushed; board 76/76; corpus sealed at kv=345 with 1336 claims; working tree clean. What this session was asked to do: audit all 1,363 corpus claims for accuracy overnight, unattended, and have a count ready in the morning. That happened. What it actually produced is more useful than a count, and less flattering. THE THREE THINGS THAT LANDED 1. The audit. All 1363 claims read — not sampled, because misframing is invisible to any mechanical scan. Four passes, 331 agents, ~30M subagent tokens: a deterministic mechanical scan, a semantic pass over every claim, an image pass reading real page photographs, and an adversarial pass that attacked the audit's own verdicts. Every artifact is at temporary/audit-2026-07-17/ (5.5 MB, gitignored) including all 312 raw agent verdict files and the 12 tools. 2. The purge. 27 claims deleted on his word; 2 rewritten instead because their defect was fixable framing sitting on correct Wallach source. 1363 → 1336, kv 343 → 344. Zero purged ids remain in any corpus artifact or in dist/main.js — they survive only in this log, which is exactly his instruction. 3. The source fix. The Epigenetics colloidal-mineral table's dropped decimals are corrected in the sealed book text, kv 344 → 345. My reading of the page came out byte-identical on 14/14 rows to the rare-earths reprint of the same assay, which had been corrected from a separate photograph. Two books, two photos, one result. THE HONEST HEADLINE The number he asked for does not exist. The audit found 109 bad claims; a skeptic pass whose only job was to destroy those flags overturned 43.5% of them. What survives is a graded list: 29 proven (27 purged, 2 rewritten), 65 needing one editorial sentence stripped, ~98 more estimated still hiding in the "clean" pile (measured, 7.8% of 90 re-read), and ~70 genuinely arguable. And the single biggest error found tonight was mine, not the corpus's. To avoid the whole-book-search trap that caused the original disaster, I scoped every auditor to the claim's own ±3500-char window — right for proving a number IS Wallach's, exactly wrong for proving one ISN'T. A 7,000-char window cannot prove a 1.5MB book never says something, and Wallach repeats himself constantly. Half the refutations found the "invented" text elsewhere in the same book. Four claims I reported to him mid-session as damning fabrications — the tuna/mercury editorial, the 1512 Monster of Ravenna, the manganese/deafness prevention, the 90/16/12/3 framework — are all in the books. On one of them the first-pass agent appended its own warning ("worth a page check") and my aggregation dropped the caveat. It flagged its uncertainty and I lost it. That lesson is now the spine of the handoff and of the memory span-presence-is-not-evidence: "he said X here" is span-scoped; "he never said X" needs the whole corpus, or it is not evidence. WHAT THE PROCESS CAUGHT THAT NARRATION WOULD NOT HAVE Both near-misses came from staging and dry-running instead of executing on his word alone. First: my own audit report's blast radius was incomplete — it enumerated emptied pages and lost Q&A but never checked the coverage GOALS, and EPIGEN-000089 (the audit's own negative control, a proven-bad claim) turned out to be the source of the live 924 mg trace/rare goal, with a dose that is CORRECT. Purging it would have reddened a critical gate to delete a right number. Second: after sealing, a purity gate went red on a book I never touched — book_purity resolves words against the CORPUS vocabulary, which is built from the claims, so deleting the only claim carrying "amebiasis" broke a gate in a different book. Root-caused and allowlisted with its citation, not baselined. FOR THE NEXT SESSION chronicle/next-chunk.md is rewritten as the authoritative handoff and points at the actual job: the ~98 unfound (highest value; needs a REDESIGNED pass with whole-book scoping for absence claims — do not just re-run the old one), the 65 editorial tails (cheap, saves claims, ruling 4), the 70 contested (judgment calls, do with him), and IMMORT-000060's word-level .txt divergence ("nitric acid" on the page vs "nitric oxide" in our source — a factual change, NOT the same class as the Flourine→Fluorine spelling normalization that landed tonight). Also carried forward: the claim_text numbers gate is designed, measured and negative-tested but NOT shipped (114 claims would fail — the real migration debt, his call); the phase1 scanner has a known false-alarm on line-wrapped spans; agent uncertainty must survive aggregation; and epigenetics is still `raw` with 3362 unresolved defects — one table was fixed, not the book. The sticky goal strip painted OVER an open drawer: its z-index came from the demo, which has no drawers. 20 -> 5, ladder documented. My first cut fixed the z-index by silently DELETING the sticky — only the measurement caught it. Both halves gated + negative-controlled.
  ↳ Luneth opened the Search drawer and the row of goal chips stayed painted on top of it. Plain version: a drawer is supposed to take over the screen, and the sticky goals strip refused to get out of its way. The cause is a clean example of a live-only integration gap. The strip's stacking number (z-index 20) came verbatim from the signed-off demo — and the demo has no drawers at all. In the demo that 20 only ever had to beat the field, so it was never tested against an overlay. Live, the Search and Knowledge drawers mount at z-index 10, and .app-workspace is position:relative with z-index:auto, which means it creates no stacking context at all — so the strip's 20 competed directly against the drawers, and won. I measured it rather than reasoned about it: with the drawer open, elementFromPoint over the strip returned SPAN.goalstrip__eyebrow with hitIsInsideDrawer=false. The strip was not merely visible on top of the drawer, it was clickable over it. The fix is z-index 20 -> 5, and I wrote the whole ladder into the stylesheet where the next reader will actually find it: the field's grid is 1 (and it is a stacking context, so everything inside it — rings at 3, tiles at 2 — is confined and 5 clears the lot), the strip is 5, the drawers are 10, the arrival veil is 60. The principle is one line: workspace chrome lives BELOW an overlay. The part worth recording is that my FIRST cut of this fix broke the sticky, and did it invisibly. The new comment prose landed outside the already-closed comment block with an orphan */, so the CSS parser dropped the declarations and the strip fell to position:static. I had fixed the z-index by deleting the sticky — repaired one half by breaking the other. Nothing errored. The board stayed green. The only thing that caught it was reading the computed style back and seeing "static" where "sticky" was expected. That is the whole argument for measuring instead of trusting the edit. TECHNICAL RECORD GATED (R7). The two facts pull in OPPOSITE directions — the strip must sit ABOVE the field so hover-focus survives a scroll, and BELOW a drawer so an overlay owns the screen — which is exactly why both are pinned rather than one. render_probe_coverage_add_remove goes 22 -> 27 checks:   · the goal strip STICKS to the workspace top after a 585px scroll (== 68px, the measured workspace top)   · the field does not scroll THROUGH the strip (the background guard)   · the Search drawer opens   · an open drawer COVERS the strip (the hit target is inside #drawer-search-mount)   · the strip is STILL position:sticky — so a future z-index fix cannot pay for itself with the sticky, the way mine just tried to NEGATIVE CONTROLS RUN. Each reproduces a REAL bug, not a hypothetical one:   · z-index restored to the demo's 20 -> REDs "an open drawer COVERS the sticky goal strip" — Luneth's reported bug, reproduced on demand.   · position:sticky -> static -> REDs both sticky checks — my own bug, reproduced on demand. ## 2026-07-15 15:09 UTC-05:00 · incident · tools
design-system.css's seal was fingerprinted over this machine's CRLF bytes — a sequence git has never stored — so the critical gate was green only here and would RED on any fresh clone as if the sealed file were tampered with. Now LF-normalized like every other seal. Re-sealed.
  ↳ The design system's stylesheet is "sealed" — we store a fingerprint of it so that if anyone tampers with it, a check goes red. But the fingerprint had been taken of the file as it sits on THIS machine, with Windows line endings, while git stores the file with Unix line endings. So the fingerprint described a version of the file git has never stored. The check passed here and nowhere else: anyone cloning the repo fresh would get a CRITICAL red screaming that a sealed file had been tampered with, when nothing had. Fixed by fingerprinting the content in a line-ending-independent way — which is what every other sealed file in the project already did. This one was the only holdout. THE SHARPEST STATEMENT OF THE BUG: the golden recorded 37c338b7..., the sha256 of the 47,691-byte CRLF working tree. The committed blob is 46,563 bytes, LF, sha256 037d0e3e.... `git ls-files --eol` says `i/lf w/crlf`, and core.autocrlf=input does not convert on checkout. So the seal was anchored to bytes that exist on exactly one disk in the world. WHAT WAS FIXED - NEW _lf_file_hash() beside _file_hash() in tools/invariants.py — sha256 of LF-normalized content, matching corpus_seal/catalog_seal/products_seal's lf_sha256(). - check_design_system_hash_integrity switched to it (call site 558 ONLY). - _file_hash DELIBERATELY LEFT RAW. It has a live second caller at line 1968: the graphics gate. eden/graphics/*.jpg are marked `binary` in .gitattributes, git never EOL-converts them, and raw bytes ARE the truth there — LF-normalizing a JPEG's hash would corrupt that seal. Changing _file_hash globally was the obvious move and would have been wrong. - The golden re-sealed 37c338b7... -> 037d0e3e.... THE CSS CONTENT WAS NOT TOUCHED: `git diff --quiet design-system.css` is clean, and the new golden EQUALS the raw sha256 of the committed blob. The seal now anchors to bytes git actually stores. - .gitattributes: dashboard/assets/styles/*.css + *.golden.sha256 pinned `text eol=lf`. This is DEFENCE IN DEPTH, not the fix — the gate is now EOL-agnostic regardless. It stops the working tree diverging from the blob again. - An EOL-aware hint added to the failure message: if the golden matches the file's RAW hash but not its LF hash, the message now says so explicitly ("a stale raw-byte seal, NOT a content edit"). A bare "hash mismatch" on a sealed canonical reads as tampering, and that misdiagnosis is expensive. - truth_anchor prose corrected. It said "raw-byte SHA-256" — accurate, and itself the defect being described. R9 — THE REFINEMENT SHIPS WITH ITS PROOF (tools/test_design_system_gates.py, 3 new cases) - eol_agnostic: the same content under LF and CRLF hashes identically AND equals the golden. This is the case the pre-fix gate fails. - content_edit_still_caught: THE NEGATIVE CONTROL, and the load-bearing half. A one-byte NON-EOL edit must STILL move the digest. Without it, "ignores line endings" could be satisfied by a function that ignores everything. A test that cannot reproduce the bug it guards proves nothing. - file_hash_still_raw: the raw hasher must still SEE an EOL difference, proving the split did not drift the binary graphics seal. - REPAIRED IN THE SAME PATCH: the pre-existing forged_hash_mismatch case patched inv._file_hash — which the fixed gate no longer calls. THE SWEEP (this was the point of auditing rather than spot-fixing): all 20 other goldens are already clone-stable, because their gates LF-normalize. Graphics raw-hashing is correct by construction. design-system was the sole holdout — so the fix adopts the existing pattern, it does not invent one. HONEST RED: invariants finished 68/69. design_system_write_protection is RED BY DESIGN — it anchors the working golden to `git show HEAD:<golden>` and reds while a golden is changed-but-uncommitted. That is the gate doing its job: it exists to catch an agent re-sealing SILENTLY, and a legitimate re-seal is supposed to be a visible, deliberate commit. It clears the moment this commit lands. Reported, not hidden, and not baselined. METHOD: found by a 37-agent adversarial audit (631 tool calls). Refuters killed several of the finders' own claims as materially overstated — including one that had the two hashes exactly backwards, and one that mis-named the gate the graphics concern applies to. Every claim's structured dose.amount must be literally present in that claim's OWN verbatim: unit-adjacent, scoped to the claim's own table row, and at the correct column index where dose.for_condition names one. ## 2026-07-14 12:10 UTC-05:00 · incident · design-system
Reduced-motion block was strobing the app at ~100Hz for the users who asked for LESS motion — capped duration but never iteration-count; 7 painted offenders measured, fixed in one line, gated by a new render probe + proven with a negative test
  ↳ Anyone whose computer is set to "reduce motion" was getting a strobing page instead of a calm one — the exact opposite of what they asked for. The rule that was supposed to quiet our animations only capped how LONG each loop lasts, never how MANY times it repeats. So a 10-second loop told to take 0.01 seconds did not stop; it ran a hundred times per second. Seven things on screen were flashing. The fix is one line. The more important part is the new probe that makes it impossible to reintroduce — this bug was invisible to every gate we had, because the CSS said the right thing and did the opposite, so reading the code could never have caught it. Only measuring the real browser could. CAUSE. design-system.css:307-318, the `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)` block, set `animation-duration: 0.01s !important` and `transition-duration: 0.01s !important` — and never set `animation-iteration-count`. Capping duration does not stop an `infinite` animation; it accelerates it 1000x. Measured headless (puppeteer, emulateMediaFeatures prefers-reduced-motion=reduce, verified honored by the browser): 7 PAINTED offenders at ~100Hz — ds-scan-sweep on .ds-scan-line (the worst: ramps opacity 0->0.35 while sweeping top from -3% to 103% across .essentials-host), ds-numeric-glow on .coverage-stat__num (the hero 13/90), ds-stat-pulse on .coverage-stat::before, ds-travel-top/-bottom on .coverage-hero::before/::after, and ds-pulse-animate on both .topbar__ask-dot and .topbar__workspace-tag::before. WCAG 2.3.1 puts the flash threshold at 3/sec. Honest severity: the scan-line is a real flash hazard (position + opacity over a large host); the other six are luminance shimmers on small or soft elements — genuinely wrong, not the same class. I am not going to inflate them. FIX. One declaration — `animation-iteration-count: 1 !important` — inside the same block. design-system.css is SEALED; user sign-off is Luneth 2026-07-14 ("1. Yes"). Golden re-sealed cdf0ebd4... -> 37c338b7..., with the CSS written BEFORE the golden so design_system_write_protection's mtime rule (css_mtime > seal_mtime + 1 = violation) holds. Verified all 7 land on a benign 100% keyframe: off-screen (ds-travel-* at left/right 130%), opacity 0 (ds-scan-sweep at top 103%), or static (ds-numeric-glow 40px/0.4, ds-pulse-animate opacity 1, ds-stat-pulse opacity 0.32). Nothing is stranded mid-animation. R7 — THE GATE SHIPS IN THE SAME PATCH. New tools/render_probe_reduced_motion.js, anchored to the RENDERED computed style in a real browser under the real media feature (§00.B #11 — pin to a truth that cannot drift). Deliberately NOT a CSS-text grep: the source declared the right intent and did the opposite, which is precisely why no existing gate saw it, and a grep would be satisfied by a reworded rule or a comment. It generalises — any future animation added anywhere that loops fast under a reduce preference reddens this probe. PASS 2 is the anti-degenerate half: deleting every animation would trivially satisfy PASS 1, so the probe also asserts the ambient motion still runs for normal users. R9 — NEGATIVE TEST. A gate that has never gone red proves nothing. Reintroduced the bug via safe_write: probe FAILED, exit 1, all 7 offenders named at ~100Hz. Restored the fix: probe PASSED, exit 0. The CSS round-tripped byte-identical (sha256 == golden: True). A MEASUREMENT LESSON WORTH KEEPING. My first probe found only 5 offenders. getComputedStyle(el) with no pseudo argument never sees ::before/::after — and 4 of the 7 live entirely on pseudo-elements. A pseudo-blind animation scan undercounts by more than half. The shipped probe scans element + ::before + ::after. VERIFIED. build exit 0 · invariants 64/64, 0 new reds (design_system_hash_integrity + design_system_write_protection both green on the new seal) · render_probe.js exit 0 with the coverage DOM unchanged (tiles 60/16/12/3, covered 14, partial 12, gap 20, stat 13/90) · render_probe_reduced_motion.js exit 0 · normal-motion regression probe: all 7 ambient animations still at authored duration + infinite. On that last one — my regression probe reported a FAIL for ds-numeric-glow because I had hardcoded 3s as its expected duration; the CSS authors it at 4s (workspace-coverage.css:330). My expectation was wrong, not the code. Recording that rather than quietly correcting the constant. CONTEXT. Found while surveying Coverage for Luneth's over-arching UX notes (goals-first flow, top-bar overhaul, the living-light mesh). This is not a Coverage change and does not touch that work, which continues next.

Phase H1 follow-up: split the flattened Table 7-8 corpus claim (RARE-000275) into 10 per-disease claims — recovers genuine ties (magnesium→hypertension, copper+sulfur→osteoporosis, boron→bone-spurs) without reopening the leak; sealed kv 320→321
  ↳ Plain: this is the first of the two data fixes the H1 fan-out surfaced. Wallach has a table (Table 7-8) that maps each degenerative disease to the mineral deficiencies that cause it — osteoporosis to calcium/magnesium/boron/copper/sulfur, hypertension to calcium/magnesium/boron, cancer to selenium, and so on. But when it was first mined, the whole table got collapsed into ONE claim listing all 10 diseases and all 10 minerals together, which throws away which mineral goes with which disease. The H1 "restore pills" rule sees a claim that broad and refuses to guess (rightly — otherwise it would tie selenium to osteoporosis and calcium to cancer). So genuine ties silently vanished. The fix is to split that one claim back into one claim per disease, exactly as the table prints it. Now each disease's page shows the right minerals, and the safety rule never had to be weakened. Table 7-8 split (Phase H1 follow-up · sealed-corpus mining · migration blueprint §1.2 over-correction class (a)). THE PROBLEM: WAL-CLM-RARE-000275 ("Table 7-8. Common Degenerative Diseases and Their Cause", Rare Earths p.169) carried conditions=[10 diseases] × essentials=[10 minerals] as flat unions — the per-disease pairing was destroyed at mining time. It is the ONLY restore-kind "shotgun" claim in the whole corpus (≥3 essentials AND ≥3 conditions), so the H1 pill rule excluded it entirely, dropping 5 genuine ties: bone_spurs→boron, hypertension→magnesium+boron, osteoporosis→copper+sulfur. Confirmed by the H1 fan-out (wf_a7ea82b2-c73). ## 2026-07-11 09:05 UTC-05:00 · round-close · redesign
Redesign D3-P2 chunk 2: the Ask-Wallach ranking/synonym pass — lay terms now resolve (blood sugar→Diabetes, quicksilver→Mercury, b12→Cobalt), results are tier-scored, and homosexuality/intersex never surface in search unless explicitly named. Signed off.
  ↳ This is the second half of the "Ask Wallach" search: making it actually understand how people type. Before, you had to type the exact name; now the search knows Wallach's own everyday words for things — so "blood sugar" brings up Diabetes, "quicksilver" brings up Mercury, "b12" brings up Cobalt, "climate" brings up Carbon — and each result quietly notes which word matched ("via 'blood sugar'"). It also ranks results sensibly and, importantly, it will NOT show the homosexuality/intersex material unless someone explicitly searches those words — that content stays in the Explore index only. Luneth signed it off. Prototype-only — temporary/knowledge-drawer-prototype.html (gitignored demo; no pillar/artifact/app code touched, board stays 53/53). Data: re-injected CLAIMS carrying the full modern-voice `answer` text (real recall — fixes "sugar cravings", which lived in the answer body I'd dropped in chunk 1) + a resolved SEARCH_ENTITIES synonym table (the 56 search entities → {slug, name, k, syn}); all 56 resolve 1:1 to the browse ESS/CONDS/TOPICS (verified 0 misses), so synonyms attach to real pages. Logic: replaced the crude all-words searchClaims with a tiered-scoring suite. apTier scores a field exact(6) › prefix(5) › word-start(4) › substring(3). nameTier weights the display name ×20, an exact element symbol =100 (so "cr" → Chromium ranks with a name-prefix, tie broken by claim count), slug words ×12. aliasTier weights a synonym ×16 (between name and slug). rankEntities scans ESS/CONDS/TOPICS by name + the SEARCH_ENTITIES synonyms, dedups by k:slug taking the max score, and tags synonym-sourced rows with a "via <synonym>" hint. rankClaims scores each claim question(12)/subject(9)/answer_short(6)/answer(4) with per-query-word coverage(+2 each) and a +8 subject-boost when the query hit an entity's name/synonym (so "blood sugar" boosts every diabetes claim). Both replace the old searchAll/searchClaims calls in apRender. Charged-content gate (Luneth's explicit ask): CHARGED = {homosexuality, intersex}. chargedExplicit(q) marks a charged subject "explicitly named" only on a strong match — the entity name exact/prefix OR an EXACT synonym ("gay", "homosexual", "same-sex attraction", "lgbt"…), never an incidental substring. rankEntities filters charged entities out unless explicit; rankClaims skips charged-subject claims unless explicit. Result: "testosterone" and "sexual" no longer pull up homosexuality; "gay"/"homosexual"/"intersex" still do. The Explore tab is EXEMPT (it doesn't use these rankers) and remains the full categorised index. Testosterone/strength reality check: the corpus genuinely has no "increase testosterone / get stronger" content yet — the only "testosterone" hits are incidental mentions inside aromatherapy/cholesterol/homosexuality claims, and sexual_health has just 1 claim. So that's a MINING gap, not a code gap; I did not fake mappings (anti-fakery). Two follow-ups captured for the search-mining phase: (1) proactively mine + tag general-interest lay topics people search — men's-health / strength / vitality with lay synonyms ("increase testosterone", "get stronger", "build muscle", "stamina", "virility") — the ranking machinery is ready and will light up the moment the data is tagged, exactly like "blood sugar" does now; (2) the charged-search-gate becomes doctrine (port to the real search build) + backfill missing synonyms like "lesbian" → homosexuality. Verified headless: a ranking probe (blood sugar→Diabetes, quicksilver→Mercury, vitamin b12→Cobalt, cr→Chromium, sugar-cravings recall) + a gate probe (testosterone / how-to-increase-testosterone / sexual → NO homosexuality-or-intersex; gay / homosexual / intersex / same-sex attraction → shown), zero page errors, plus a screenshot of the "blood sugar → Diabetes (via 'blood sugar')" win. Three rules: (1) trail[0] is ALWAYS {tab:'home',label:'Home'} — replaces the old section-tab root that could go stale once you branch across essential↔condition; goCrumb() already routes a tab-crumb to close the detail, so the Home crumb exits cleanly to the Home tab. (3) capTrail() splices index 1 (the oldest recent crumb — never Home[0], never the current tail) until length ≤ CRUMB_MAX, i.e. Home + 5 most-recent; CRUMB_MAX is a one-line tunable (5–8) at line 418.
